key_patterns.name: Heterogeneous baseline propensity via risk_perception
key_patterns.description: Agents have continuous risk_perception in [0,1], which maps to higher initial adoption and higher responsiveness to peer influence.
key_patterns.relevance: Enables realistic heterogeneity; needed for micro-level adoption probabilities and stratified calibration.

key_patterns.name: Multiplex social structure with layer-dependent influence
key_patterns.description: Three layers (family, work_school, community) with different expected tie densities and interaction intensities; family ties are fewer but stronger, community more numerous but weaker.
key_patterns.relevance: Supports layer-specific contact and influence weights; critical to reproduce adoption speed and peak.

key_patterns.name: Homophily by age_group and occupation
key_patterns.description: Edges likely assortative within age_group/occupation (especially work_school for occupation and family for age proximity).
key_patterns.relevance: Homophily shapes local clustering of adoption and inequalities; informs mixing matrices and group-specific calibration.

key_patterns.name: Behavioral inertia (habit persistence)
key_patterns.description: wearing_mask tends to persist day-to-day once adopted (state dependence).
key_patterns.relevance: Requires a persistence parameter to reproduce final adoption and peak width.

key_patterns.name: Information precedes adoption
key_patterns.description: received_info acts as a trigger or booster for subsequent mask adoption.
key_patterns.relevance: Model should separate information diffusion from behavioral adoption and include coupling between them.

key_patterns.name: Network centrality and early adoption
key_patterns.description: Higher-degree agents (especially in work_school/community) likely adopt earlier due to higher exposure.
key_patterns.relevance: Affects time_to_50_percent and peak_adoption; can guide seeding strategies and centrality-weighted influence.

key_patterns.name: Group-level inequality in adoption
key_patterns.description: Adoption rates vary by age_group and occupation, driven by homophily and trait heterogeneity.
key_patterns.relevance: Directly tied to the adoption_inequality_gini metric; informs group modifiers.

key_distributions.name: Risk perception distribution
key_distributions.description: Continuous on [0,1]; typically right- or left-skewed depending on population; fit with a Beta distribution.
key_distributions.parameters: alpha, beta estimated from agent_attributes.csv: let mean=m and variance=v over risk_perception; alpha=m*(m*(1-m)/v - 1), beta=(1-m)*(m*(1-m)/v - 1)

key_distributions.name: Layer-specific degree distributions
key_distributions.description: Family: low-degree narrow distribution; Work/School: moderate variance; Community: heavy-tailed.
key_distributions.parameters: Fit Poisson or Negative Binomial per layer from the multiplex JSON. For NB: mean=k*(1-p)/p and variance=mean/p; estimate (k, p) by MLE.

key_distributions.name: Daily adoption trajectory
key_distributions.description: Population adoption over time resembles a logistic/S-curve with possible plateaus from policy shocks.
key_distributions.parameters: Logistic: A(t)=K/(1+exp(-g*(t-t0))). Estimate K (carrying capacity), g (growth rate), t0 (inflection) by NLS on panel daily means.

key_distributions.name: Information arrival times
key_distributions.description: Time-to-received_info per agent; can be modeled as competing hazards from each layer plus exogenous media.
key_distributions.parameters: Layer hazards λ_family, λ_work_school, λ_community and exogenous λ_media estimated via discrete-time survival on received_info.

key_distributions.name: Exposure distribution (peer mask fraction)
key_distributions.description: Daily distribution of the fraction of neighbors wearing masks per agent per layer.
key_distributions.parameters: Empirical per-layer mean and variance; optionally approximate as Beta(a_l, b_l) via method of moments.

key_relationships.relationship: Higher risk_perception increases the probability of adopting and reduces time to adoption.
key_relationships.strength: Expected strong; quantify via logistic coefficient magnitude and significance.

key_relationships.relationship: Having received information increases next-day adoption probability, controlling for prior state.
key_relationships.strength: Strong; estimate via discrete-time hazard model.

key_relationships.relationship: Higher fraction of family members wearing masks increases adoption likelihood.
key_relationships.strength: Strongest among layers due to tie strength.

key_relationships.relationship: Work/school peers’ adoption drives adoption via conformity.
Community exposure influences adoption through norms/visibility.
Assortative mixing creates pockets of high or low adoption.
State persistence; adopters tend to remain adopters.
key_relationships.strength: Strong; high odds ratio or transition probability.

symmetrize_edges.source: Multiplex JSON (edge lists may be asymmetric)
symmetrize_edges.notes: Create undirected graphs per layer; remove self-loops; deduplicate neighbors.

layer_overlap_policy.notes: If a tie appears in multiple layers, keep a single edge with weight equal to the sum of layer weights; retain layer tags for exposure accounting.

degree_distribution_family.notes: Estimate mean degree and choose Poisson if variance≈mean; else NB.

degree_distribution_work_school.notes: Use MLE for NB parameters (k, p); capture overdispersion.

degree_distribution_community.notes: Test NB vs truncated power law; choose by AIC/BIC.

assortativity_by_age.notes: Compute Newman assortativity r per layer to parameterize homophily.

assortativity_by_occupation.notes: Used to validate mixing patterns in generated or pruned networks.

w_family.source: Recommended prior; to be tuned with panel data
w_family.notes: Relative influence/contact intensity multiplier for family vs community.

w_work_school.source: Recommended prior; to be tuned with panel data

w_community.notes: Set baseline scaling; others relative to this.

adoption_model.notes: P(adopt_t=1 | state_{t-1}) = sigmoid(alpha + gamma_r*risk + beta_f*peer_frac_f + beta_w*peer_frac_w + beta_c*peer_frac_c + delta*received_info + phi*prev_adopter)

alpha_intercept.notes: Sets baseline adoption without exposure; tune to match initial slope.

gamma_risk_perception.source: Recommended initial; estimate via logistic on panel

beta_peer_family.source: Recommended initial; estimate via logistic with layer exposures
beta_peer_family.notes: Effect per unit fraction of family adopters.

beta_peer_work_school.source: Recommended initial; estimate via logistic with layer exposures
beta_peer_work_school.notes: Effect per unit fraction of work/school adopters.

beta_peer_community.source: Recommended initial; estimate via logistic with layer exposures
beta_peer_community.notes: Effect per unit fraction of community adopters.

delta_received_info.notes: Additive boost in log-odds when info received.

phi_persistence.source: Recommended initial; estimate via logistic on prior_wearing_mask
phi_persistence.notes: Log-odds effect for previous-day adoption; translates to high persistence.

recovery_or_dropout_prob.source: Recommended initial; estimate via transition counts
recovery_or_dropout_prob.notes: Daily probability that an adopter stops wearing a mask absent exposure; controls peak width.

p_info_contact_family.source: Recommended prior; estimate via discrete-time survival on received_info
p_info_contact_family.notes: Per-contact probability of info transmission in family.

lambda_media_daily.source: Recommended prior; estimate from baseline hazard of received_info among isolates
lambda_media_daily.notes: Exogenous daily probability of receiving info.

age_group_modifier.source: agent_attributes.csv; tune to match group adoption curves
age_group_modifier.notes: Multiplicative factor on social influence terms to capture group conformity differences.

occupation_modifier.source: agent_attributes.csv; tune to match occupation-stratified adoption
occupation_modifier.notes: Multiplicative factor on social influence terms.

risk_perception_distribution.notes: Fit alpha_hat and beta_hat from empirical mean/variance; sample per agent if generating synthetic agents.

initial_adoption_rate.notes: Initialize mask state by sampling to match empirical day-0 rate or by using exact day-0 states if simulating observed agents.

seeding_rule.notes: If not using observed day-0 states, seed adopters among top quantiles of risk_perception and degree to match early adoption slope.

gini_grouping_dimension.notes: Compute adoption_inequality_gini across age groups at specified time (e.g., final day).

metrics_weights_for_loss.notes: Weights for multi-objective loss; adjust per policy focus.

preprocessing_steps.purpose: Ensure agent_id alignment across agent_attributes.csv, multiplex JSON, and panel time-series; cast IDs to int; validate referential integrity.
Symmetrize edges, remove self-loops, deduplicate neighbors, construct per-layer graphs, compute degrees, clustering, assortativity.
Assign initial layer weights (w_family, w_work_school, w_community); create combined weighted adjacency if using merged layer model.
For each agent-day, compute peer_mask_fraction per layer (lagged), and total exposure counts to use in micro-level regression.
Compute daily population adoption rate, group-specific adoption rates (age_group, occupation), and identify calibration and validation windows.
Fit Beta(alpha, beta) to risk_perception for use in synthetic population generation or to inform heterogeneity scaling.
Impute or drop missing wearing_mask/received_info; enforce logical constraints (e.g., once received_info=true remains true if cumulative).

calibration_strategy.calibration_approach: Use a two-stage, micro-to-macro calibration. Stage 1 (micro): Fit a discrete-time logistic hazard model on panel data with predictors: prior_wearing_mask, received_info, risk_perception, and layer-specific peer_mask_fraction (lagged). Include random intercepts by age_group/occupation to estimate heterogeneity modifiers and persistence (phi). Extract initial parameter estimates: alpha, gamma_r, beta_f, beta_w, beta_c, delta, phi. Estimate information diffusion hazards via survival analysis for received_info using layer exposure counts and an exogenous baseline hazard (lambda_media). Stage 2 (macro): Run the multi-agent simulation with Stage 1 parameters as priors. Calibrate remaining parameters and refine all via simulation-based optimization to match population-level targets: minimize a weighted loss over RMSE_adoption and MAE_adoption with penalties for discrepancies in peak_adoption, time_to_50_percent, final_adoption, and adoption_inequality_gini. Use Bayesian Optimization or CMA-ES over parameter space {w_family, w_work_school, w_community, alpha, gamma_r, beta_f, beta_w, beta_c, delta, phi, p_info_contact_* , lambda_media, group modifiers}. Optionally incorporate Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC-SMC) to obtain parameter posteriors.
calibration_strategy.validation_strategy: Temporal holdout: fit on first 70% of days; validate on last 30%. Compute all metrics on validation window. Stratified validation: compute adoption curves and errors by age_group and occupation; verify adoption_inequality_gini at final day and at mid-trajectory. Network validation: check that simulated degree-exposure relationships reproduce observed early-adoption vs degree patterns. Sensitivity analysis: perform global (Sobol) sensitivity to rank drivers of RMSE_adoption and time_to_50_percent; perform local one-at-a-time on layer weights. Posterior predictive checks: replicate distribution of daily changes in adoption and transition matrices (adopt->stay/leave). Robustness: re-run with directed vs undirected edges and with/without layer overlap merging to confirm qualitative stability.

file_summaries:
Semantic metadata summary for agent_attributes.csv

- Structure and type
  - Tabular CSV; one row per agent (no nesting).
  - Columns: agent_id (int), age_group (categorical), occupation (categorical), risk_perception (float in [0,1]).

- Column meanings
  - agent_id: Unique primary key for each agent; used to join with network/edge lists and state tables.
  - age_group: Demographic stratum (e.g., Youth, Young Adult, Middle Age); can drive homophily, contact patterns, and compliance modifiers.
  - occupation: Socio-role category (e.g., Student, White Collar, Blue Collar); informs context-specific mixing (school, workplace), contact rates, and policy effects.
  - risk_perception: Individual-level latent trait in [0,1] reflecting perceived disease risk; seeds heterogeneity in initial mask adoption and responsiveness to social influence or public information.

- Relationships or nested elements
  - No nested fields; each record is independent.
  - Implicit groupings: agents can be clustered by age_group and occupation; agent_id links externally to social network edges and time-varying states (e.g., mask_wearing).

- How to use in the simulation
  - Initialize agents: create one agent per row with static attributes (age_group, occupation) and a continuous trait (risk_perception).
  - Adoption propensity: map risk_perception to baseline mask adoption probability or threshold (e.g., logistic or threshold model).
  - Social influence heterogeneity: weight peer influence by risk_perception and allow age/occupation-specific susceptibility or conformity parameters.
  - Contact structure: use age_group and occupation to:
    - Generate homophilous networks or layered contacts (household/school/work/community).
    - Assign contact rates and context-specific transmission of behavior.
  - Policy/communication targeting: enable interventions stratified by age_group/occupation or by low/high risk_perception.
  - Analytics: stratify outcomes and calibrate parameters by these categories; agent_id supports joins with dynamic behavior logs and network files.

Semantic metadata summary (for mask-wearing diffusion simulation)

- Overall data structure and type
  - JSON object (dictionary) where each top-level entry represents one individual (agent).
  - Each agent maps to a nested object partitioning their social ties into multiple layers.

- Meaning of keys or columns
  - Top-level keys: stringified integer agent IDs (e.g., "0", "1"). Treat as unique agent identifiers; normalize to int or keep as strings consistently.
  - Nested keys: relationship layers
    - family: close-kin ties
    - work_school: coworkers/classmates
    - community: broader community contacts
  - Values of each nested key: arrays of integer IDs referencing other agents in the same ID space.

- Relationships or nested elements
  - Multiplex (multi-layer) adjacency lists: each agent has up to three neighbor lists, one per social context.
  - Edges are unweighted and static in the file; no timestamps or frequencies provided.
  - Directionality is unspecified; lists may be asymmetric. Decide to:
    - treat as directed, or
    - symmetrize during preprocessing (recommended if modeling mutual ties).
  - Possible data hygiene needs: deduplicate neighbor lists, ensure all referenced IDs exist as nodes, handle empty lists (isolates), and decide how to treat contacts that appear in multiple layers (as distinct parallel ties vs. merged with summed weight).

- How this data should inform simulation entities or interactions
  - Agents: instantiate one agent per top-level ID with a mask state (e.g., adopter/non-adopter), propensity/susceptibility parameters, and per-layer exposure tallies.
  - Network: build three layer-specific graphs (family, work_school, community) or a single multiplex graph with an edge attribute for layer.
  - Interaction scheduling: at each time step, sample interactions per layer; layer-specific contact rates should reflect typical intensity (e.g., family > work_school > community) and can be parameterized since the file has no weights.
  - Influence dynamics: compute adoption pressure from neighbors within each layer; apply layer-specific influence weights or probabilities to update mask-wearing behavior.
  - Calibration hooks: initial seeding of adopters, optional symmetrization, optional assignment of per-layer weights/contact frequencies, and handling of overlapping ties across layers.

- Overall data structure and type:
  - CSV, panel time-series at daily granularity.
  - Each row is the state of one agent on one day.

- Meaning of keys/columns:
  - day (int): discrete timestep (0-indexed). Defines simulation step size (1 day).
  - agent_id (int): unique agent identifier; links rows across days.
  - wearing_mask (bool): agent’s behavioral state at that day.
  - received_info (bool): whether the agent has been exposed to mask-related information by that day (exogenous or via network).

- Relationships or nested elements:
  - No nesting; flat table.
  - Longitudinal relation: multiple rows per agent across days form a trajectory.
  - Potential external relation: agent_id can be joined to a social network (adjacency/edge list) not present here.

- How this data should inform simulation entities or interactions:
  - Agent schema: for each agent, maintain state variables wearing_mask and received_info, updated each day.
  - Initialization: use day 0 rows for initial states; if later days exist, they provide ground truth for calibration/validation.
  - Dynamics/calibration:
    - Learn or set transition probabilities P(wearing_mask_t | wearing_mask_{t-1}, received_info_t, neighbors’ states).
    - Use received_info as a prerequisite or booster for adoption (e.g., higher adoption probability when received_info = true).
    - Use trajectories to estimate parameters such as baseline adoption, social influence strength, and persistence (habit/inertia).
  - Network interactions: propagate received_info (and possibly social influence on wearing_mask) via a separate social graph using agent_id; this file alone does not specify edges.
  - Simulation step = 1 day; iterate over agents each step, first update info exposure via network, then update mask-wearing based on exposure and peer influence.
